expected.introduction: How did an expedition relate to the establishment of colonial rule? Arrival, settlement and effective control are different developments. Distinguishing them makes historical change easier to explain.
expected.title: Legazpi's Expedition
expected.lessonRecap: Legazpi's 1564 departure and the 1565 Cebu settlement belong to a later expedition, distinct from Magellan's voyage. Command, navigation knowledge and Spanish aims were distinct. Plans and responsibilities do not establish universal consent or success. Local opposition, force and a recorded agreement all belong in the account. A leader's agreement is not proof of everyone's consent. The Spanish base was a continuing presence within an existing community. Its establishment was not proof of instant control everywhere. The return connection helped communication and supplies. Navigation and crew work mattered, but a route did not guarantee safety or universal control.

expected.title: A Later Expedition, a Different Stage
expected.contentReviewStatus: Source-informed draft; independent teacher, curriculum alignment and Grade 5 review pending
expected.content:
Chapter 5 ended with later voyages and a question: when does a visit become an attempt to maintain colonial rule? Chapter 6 begins with Miguel Lopez de Legazpi's expedition. This was a later journey, not Magellan's fleet returning under a different name.

Legazpi's expedition departed from Mexico, then part of New Spain, in 1564. It crossed the Pacific and reached the Philippine islands in 1565. After visiting several places, it established a Spanish settlement in Cebu that year. Existing communities and their histories were already there.

Watch how to read the timeline. First identify what the date labels: departure or a later event. Next connect the places in a selected sequence. Finally state a limit: the line omits many stops and does not show exact sailing directions, distance or everyone's experience.

Compare this with your earlier work. Magellan died in 1521; Legazpi's 1564-1565 expedition was much later. Keep leaders, journeys and events separate before explaining how the colonial presence developed.
expected.historicalInsight: Legazpi's expedition was distinct from Magellan's earlier voyage and from Elcano's return.

fields.title: Put the later voyage in order
fields.content:
Miguel Lopez de Legazpi led a later expedition, separate from Magellan’s. It departed Mexico, then part of New Spain, in 1564 and crossed the Pacific to the Philippine islands in 1565.

A Spanish settlement was established in Cebu in 1565, among existing communities. Read each timeline label: leaving, arriving and establishing a base are different events. The line shows selected events, not every stop or exact sailing direction.

expected.title: Aims and Different Responsibilities
expected.content:
A voyage has aims and people with different responsibilities. The Spanish Crown sought to occupy the islands and establish a continuing presence. A workable return connection across the Pacific also mattered. These were the sponsor's aims, not proof that communities had accepted them.

Legazpi commanded the expedition. Andres de Urdaneta, an Augustinian friar with earlier Pacific experience, contributed navigation knowledge and helped with the return route. A friar is a member of a religious community. We study his role as history; students are not asked to adopt his religion.

Try a fictional team-record task. One card describes command, another describes navigation knowledge, and a third describes the sponsor's aims. Put each in the right column. Do not give a single person credit for every action by the crews or erase the people who already lived at the destinations.

An aim tells what was wanted. A responsibility tells who undertook a task. An outcome tells what happened. Keeping these separate helps you evaluate the expedition rather than assume every plan succeeded.

fields.title: Different people, different responsibilities
fields.content:
The Spanish Crown sought occupation and a continuing presence. A workable Pacific return connection also mattered. These aims do not show that local communities accepted them.

Legazpi commanded. Andres de Urdaneta was an Augustinian friar with earlier Pacific experience who contributed navigation knowledge. A friar belongs to a religious community; learning his historical role does not require sharing his faith.

expected.content:
The expedition arrived among communities with their own leaders and interests. Local people could negotiate, provide supplies or resist. An account about the newcomers alone cannot explain the whole encounter.

Establishing the Spanish presence in Cebu involved force and local opposition, not simply an invitation from every resident. A historical marker in Cebu also records an agreement between Rajah Tupas and Legazpi in 1565. A later agreement and earlier conflict can both be part of the history. Do not turn either into the feelings of every individual.

Read a fictional exhibit claim: One recorded agreement proves everyone freely supported the whole colonial project. Check the leap. Who participated? What did the agreement address? What pressure or conflict surrounded it? More evidence is needed for a statement about all residents.

A treaty record can help explain a formal relationship. It cannot reveal every private motive or stand for every community in the archipelago. Name local participants and distinguish a recorded action from an unsupported claim of universal consent.

expected.keyTermDefinition: A place where people establish a continuing base to live.
expected.content:
A settlement is a place where people establish a continuing base to live. The Spanish settlement in Cebu in 1565 differed from a brief visit. Maintaining that presence required supplies, organization and relationships with people in the region.

This did not mean Legazpi created Cebu. Its trading community and local leadership existed before the expedition. Use precise wording: a Spanish settlement was established in an already inhabited place. Saying Cebu began in 1565 would erase earlier history.

Work through a fictional evidence table. A ship arriving supports a claim of arrival. Records of a maintained base support a claim of continuing presence there. Neither alone proves effective authority over every island. To investigate that larger claim, ask where institutions operated, how people responded and what limits remained.

The next missions examine settlements in Cebu and Manila and the expansion of colonial control. Here, explain the first step without jumping to the end: one settlement mattered, but colonial rule developed unevenly and did not become universal on a single day.

expected.content:
Reaching the islands did not answer every question about staying connected across the Pacific. A return route mattered for carrying news, people and supplies. Trade also depended on continuing connections, not just one arrival.

In 1565, the San Pedro made a return voyage from Cebu to Mexico. Urdaneta contributed navigation knowledge, while Felipe de Salcedo captained the ship and other navigators and crew carried out the journey. Winds and currents helped shape the route. The journey was a team effort, not one person sailing alone.

The return is often discussed as the tornaviaje. We use that word here for the return journey. Do not turn it into a claim that no other person ever attempted or completed a Pacific crossing. This scene does not settle every question about priority among voyages.

Use the diagram as a sequence, not sailing directions. Then explain a connection: a workable return could help support communication and continued presence. It did not guarantee safety on every voyage, erase local resistance or by itself prove control across the archipelago.

expected.content:
Build an explanation that connects the expedition with the beginning of a continuing Spanish presence. Keep the 1564 departure and the events of 1565 distinct. Separate Legazpi's command from Urdaneta's navigation work and the work of other participants.

Include local responses. Conflict, pressure and an agreement with named leaders cannot be reduced to one opinion held by every resident. Describe the settlement as a Spanish base in an existing community, and connect the return journey with communication and supplies.

expected.title: Two Settlements, Two Dates
expected.content:
In Mission 1, you investigated Legazpi's expedition. Now compare two places where a continuing Spanish presence developed: Cebu and Manila. Comparing means using the same questions for both places, rather than treating them as identical.

A Spanish settlement was established in Cebu in 1565. A Spanish city was established in Manila in 1571. These dates describe colonial developments in places where people already lived, traded and made decisions. They do not mean that the places or their histories began with Spanish arrival.

Watch how to build a comparison. Put Cebu and Manila in separate columns. Under each, write the year of the colonial development. Next add a question about the existing community and another about local responses. This makes the date a starting point for explanation rather than the whole story.

Keep the events in order: Cebu's 1565 settlement came before Manila's 1571 Spanish city. The diagram is a selected comparison, not a complete travel itinerary or proof that every island between the two came under control.

expected.content:
A phrase such as founding a city can hide an important question: whose city, and what existed before? People did not appear only when a colonial government was established.

Cebu already had a trading community and local leaders. A Cebu historical marker records Rajah Tupas in an agreement with Legazpi in 1565. In the Manila area, Maynila was associated with Rajah Sulayman, whose name is also written Soliman. The Intramuros Administration describes the later Spanish city as established on the site of the earlier polity. A polity is a community organized under political authority.

Try a fictional museum-label task. A label says that Spanish officials created all leadership and trade in both places. Check the evidence of earlier communities and named leaders. Revise the label to distinguish an existing society from a new colonial institution.

Naming a leader does not reveal every resident's views or tell the complete history of the community. It does help correct the idea that these were empty places waiting for outsiders to begin their history.

expected.content:
A port is a place where ships can arrive and exchange people or goods with the shore. A useful landing place matters, but trade also needs people, knowledge, supplies and relationships. Location alone does not do the trading.

Cebu was already connected with exchange before the Spanish base. Manila became important to Spanish plans because of its position and connections with Asian trade. The Library of Congress discussion explains how regional merchants helped connect Spanish newcomers with trade centered in Luzon. Existing traders were participants, not simply resources discovered by outsiders.

Watch how to read the port model. Find the sea connection, the landing area and the community. Connect each feature to an action: goods must be carried, exchanged or stored by people. Then state the limit: this teaching model does not reconstruct either port's exact buildings or prove an uninterrupted route between them.

For your comparison, explain how connections and human activity mattered in both places. A promising location did not guarantee profit, local consent or control of every trading relationship.

expected.decisionSituation: Which report uses the local-response evidence carefully?
expected.content:
A continuing colonial presence could meet negotiation, pressure and resistance. These responses could differ across places and change over time. A report should not give everyone one opinion.

In Cebu, the recorded agreement involving Tupas belongs alongside the conflict studied in Mission 1. Around Manila Bay, the NHCP Bangkusay marker records resistance by communities and a force led by a leader from Macabebe in 1571. This shows that establishing a Spanish city did not mean that all nearby communities accepted the newcomers' authority.

Be careful with identities. Do not turn the Macabebe leader named by place in the marker into Rajah Sulayman merely because Sulayman is a familiar name in Manila's history. The evidence must support the identity as well as the event. No invented speech is needed to explain that communities resisted.

Try a fictional report check. A student uses one agreement to claim everyone welcomed colonial rule. Another uses one battle to claim every community responded identically. Revise both: name the action, its participants and the limit on what it tells us.

expected.decisionSituation: What evidence would help check the reach of an order issued from a colonial base?
expected.content:
A colonial settlement could provide a base for officials, supplies and armed forces. Manila became a center of Spanish colonial government. Legazpi established a city council there in 1571. A council is a group with responsibilities for governing a town or city.

An institution is an organized body with continuing duties. Establishing one is different from simply visiting a shore. But an official's claim of authority is also different from evidence that people followed it everywhere.

Use a fictional worked example. A council records an order. To investigate its effects, ask where it was carried out, who supplied resources, how people responded and where it was resisted or could not be enforced. The written order proves the order was issued; it does not answer all these later questions.

Compare Cebu and Manila as bases for the colonial presence without drawing a circle around every island and calling it controlled. Later missions examine expansion, methods and limits in more detail. Here, connect the purpose of a base with the people, resources and responses that shaped its actual reach.

expected.content:
You have compared Cebu and Manila as colonial bases. Now ask how officials tried to extend authority beyond a base. Issuing an order was only one step. People had to carry messages, obtain supplies and make decisions in the places affected. Existing trade connections and local relationships mattered.

The Library of Congress discussion of early colonial history describes the importance of regional merchants and local interests. These connections could support a continuing Spanish presence, but did not make every community accept it. A base was a starting point for attempts to expand authority, not proof of success everywhere.

Read the link diagram as a thinking guide. For each arrow, ask what action and whose work connected the places. It is not an exact route map or a complete account of expansion.

expected.content:
Expansion could involve force and pressure as well as agreements. Coercion means trying to make someone obey through threats or force. An official might describe an action as peaceful even when affected people faced serious pressure. Read the action and its setting, not just a favorable label.

The Cebu and Mactan lessons supplied named examples of demands and conflict. Use them as background, without assuming every later place followed the same sequence. Explaining how coercion worked is different from approving it. We do not earn points for harm in this investigation.

Try a fictional comparison. One card records a request; another adds a threat if it is refused. Ask what changed. A reply under pressure cannot automatically be treated as evidence that every person freely welcomed outside rule. The cards help you reason; they do not quote historical participants.

exploreItems.hint: Look for an idea and a limit.

exploreItems.title: Resistance
exploreItems.hint: Look for an idea and a limit.

expected.content:
People responded to colonial demands in different ways. Negotiation means discussing terms. Adaptation means changing some practices in response to circumstances. Resistance means opposing a demand or an attempt to impose authority. These are actions to investigate, not permanent labels for whole peoples.

A community could negotiate at one time and resist a different demand later. People within a place could also have different interests. Do not assume one leader's action reveals every person's thoughts. Your earlier Cebu agreement and Manila Bay resistance examples show why separate settings need separate evidence.

expected.content:
A claim of authority can be wider than its practical reach. To check effective control, investigate whether decisions were carried out and what people did in response. A colored area on a modern teaching map cannot answer all those questions.

Travel conditions and supplies affected contact, but terrain alone did not decide history. Local organization, knowledge, alliances and resistance mattered too. Avoid calling a community backward because it maintained its own leadership. Different relationships with colonial institutions do not rank people's worth.

Work through a fictional case: an order is issued, but the record gives no evidence of its delivery or enforcement in another place. You may report that an order was issued. You need more evidence to claim it was followed there. Keep time and place attached to your conclusion, because authority could expand, weaken or be contested.

expected.keyTermDefinition: The ability of a community to make and maintain its own decisions.
expected.content:
Did colonial claims erase every form of local authority? Named examples help test that idea. National Museum material describing research in Ifugao explains resistance to Spanish conquest. This is an example of local organization and agency, not proof that every highland community had an identical history.

NCCA's history of Muslim communities discusses diplomacy and conflict involving the Sulu sultanate and Spanish officials, including a treaty in 1726. This later example shows why we must keep periods distinct. It is not an event from Legazpi's 1565 expedition. Diplomacy does not by itself prove that all parties understood terms identically or that conflict never occurred.

Compare the examples without turning Ifugao or Sulu into timeless, uniform groups. Both help question universal-control claims, but they involve different settings. Chapter 11 will develop these histories; this mission introduces the evidence question rather than covering them completely.

expected.content:
Build an explanation rather than color an entire archipelago as controlled. Start with a base and the connections needed to act beyond it. Identify whether the evidence describes a request, pressure, an agreement or force. Name a local response and keep the issue, place and time attached.

Then check the result. An order is evidence of a decision being issued, not automatically of its enforcement everywhere. Different communities and different periods need their own evidence. The Ifugao and Sulu examples introduce distinct histories; neither supplies one response for all people.

Use this fictional report frame: Officials attempted [action]. At [place and time], people responded by [supported action]. The evidence shows [effect], but does not establish [unsupported claim]. This is a classroom guide, not an original speech.

expected.title: The Meaning, Motives, and Methods of Colonization
expected.introduction: What makes colonization different from a visit or exchange? Recognising imposed authority helps us examine power, methods and effects without confusing contact with control.
expected.learningObjective: Explain colonization by separating meaning, motives, methods, effects and source viewpoints.
expected.lessonRecap: Colonization concerns continuing outside authority. A visit, name or claim alone does not establish its actual reach. Imperial motives could include economic, political and religious aims. A desired result is not an achieved result or a justification. Methods are actions or arrangements used to pursue an aim. Their operation and effects need place-specific evidence. Investigate consequences for particular people using evidence. An official aim does not substitute for effects or local responses. Identify aims, methods and effects separately. Evidence of an institution alone cannot establish universal enforcement or consent.

fields.lessonRecap: Colonization involves establishing and maintaining outside authority over a place and its people, beyond a visit or exchange. Economic, political and religious aims were motives; they do not prove results or justify domination. Methods are actions used to pursue aims: force, agreements, offices and religious institutions. Their operation varied. Effects concern consequences for particular people. Intended benefits do not establish everyone’s actual experience. An institution’s creation does not establish universal enforcement, consent or happiness. Separate the source’s claim from what it proves.

expected.content:
An expedition is a journey. A settlement is a continuing base. Colonization involves an outside power establishing and maintaining authority over a place and its people. These ideas connect, but they are not interchangeable. A ship arriving or a new name appearing in an account does not alone establish continuing rule.

Your Cebu and Manila investigations showed colonial bases in existing societies. People already had leaders, connections and histories. Explaining colonization should identify the outside authority and how it attempted to organize power over people, without treating the communities as empty land.

Try a fictional report check. One card describes a passing ship. Another describes outside officials establishing continuing governing duties. Ask which action supports a claim about colonial rule and what further evidence would show its actual reach. The cards are teaching examples, not original records.

A definition helps classify the claim; evidence still determines what happened in each place.

expected.title: Why Did Sponsors Seek Rule?
expected.imageAlt: A modern comparison guide for Why Did Sponsors Seek Rule?. It separates evidence categories and their limits; it is not an original historical image, speech or map.
expected.historicalInsight: Identifying a motive does not justify coercion or establish every resident's consent.
expected.content:
Motives explain why people or institutions sought an action. Spanish imperial plans included economic interests, political power and religious aims. Trade access, influence and spreading Catholic Christianity could be connected, but this does not mean every participant had identical priorities.

The Philippine Embassy in Madrid's historical discussion identifies religious, economic and geopolitical motives. Geopolitical means connected with power and relationships between places. Use these as categories for questions, not as a formula that reads everyone's private thoughts.

Watch how to check a fictional sponsor card. If it says a sponsor wants access to trade, identify an economic aim. Do not write that the aim proves a profitable result or makes domination acceptable. Naming a religious aim also does not establish that everyone adopted the religion.

Students can study these aims without practising a faith. Explain a motive with a source and keep it separate from the method used and the result achieved.

expected.content:
A method is a way of trying to achieve an aim. Colonial authority could be pursued through force, agreements, governing offices and religious institutions. These could interact. Their exact operation varied across places and periods.

The DepEd learning resource lists military force, tribute, encomienda and compulsory labor among topics for investigating subjection to Spanish authority. This mission introduces the categories; later chapters examine the systems and their changing rules. Tribute means a required payment to an authority. Naming it here does not establish who paid what amount in every place.

Try sorting a fictional report. Wanting influence is an aim. Creating an office that issues decisions is a method. Evidence about what happened to families afterward concerns effects. A payment demand is not automatically a freely chosen gift.

Check the action rather than judging by an official's favorable label. A recorded agreement needs its participants and context, especially where force or pressure was involved.

fields.title: Aim, method or effect?
fields.content:
A method is a way of pursuing an aim. Colonial methods could include force, agreements, governing offices and religious institutions. DepEd’s learning resource also identifies tribute, encomienda and compulsory labor for investigation in later lessons.

Tribute is a required payment to authority. Try a fictional sort: wanting influence is an aim, creating an office is a method, and what happens to families is an effect. A required payment is not automatically a freely chosen gift. Exact obligations need evidence for the place and period.

expected.keyTermDefinition: A consequence of an action, event or arrangement.
expected.content:
An effect is a consequence of an action or arrangement. Effects are not always the outcomes sponsors intended. Asking what changed must include the people affected, not just whether an official achieved a goal.

A required payment could place demands on household resources. To explain its actual effect, check evidence of the requirement, collection and families' circumstances. Do not invent a single amount or burden for every community. People could negotiate, adapt or resist, as you studied in Mission 3.

Use a fictional family-record exercise. A record notes that goods were collected and that a household had fewer goods afterward. This supports a particular consequence in that example. More evidence is needed for a claim that all families had exactly that experience or that we know everyone's thoughts.

Compare different perspectives: an official may describe revenue, while affected people experience obligations. A report can examine both without treating the official account as the only story or making all local responses identical.

expected.keyTermDefinition: The position and interests reflected in an account.
expected.content:
A source can describe aims, methods or effects, but it may emphasize one viewpoint. An official report saying a policy brought peace does not by itself show that every person freely accepted it. Compare its claim with evidence of actions and local responses.

The Library of Congress account of early colonial relationships highlights local interests and negotiation alongside Spanish aims and coercion. It helps us ask whose participation and choices are missing from a simple story of one-sided control. This does not mean every account is useless; it means a claim must fit what the source can establish.

Work through a fictional exhibit caption: A new office was created, so all islands happily obeyed. The first clause describes an institution. The second adds claims about reach and feelings that need separate evidence. Correct the caption instead of inventing a speech to support it.

Explaining colonization is not a game of choosing which people are worth more. Use evidence, name harms and keep uncertainty visible without erasing anyone's history.

A source may emphasize aims, methods or effects from one viewpoint. Compare its claims with actions and local responses rather than treating an official report as everyone’s story.

expected.historicalInsight: Use local evidence, identify the source viewpoint and avoid inventing universal consent.
expected.imageCaption: Modern teaching diagram, not an original historical source.
expected.content:
Complete your explanation using three connected questions. What did an authority seek? What actions or institutions were used? What happened to the people affected? Keep colonization's continuing outside authority distinct from a brief visit, and keep earlier local histories visible.

Use a named example from this chapter without turning it into a universal pattern. Settlements, connections, demands and local responses must be explained in their settings. An aim does not guarantee an outcome. A method does not establish everyone's consent. A particular effect does not describe all families.

Try this fictional report frame in your own words: The stated aim was [aim]. The action used was [method]. Evidence about [people, place and time] shows [effect or response]. It does not establish [unsupported claim]. The frame is a classroom tool, not an original speech.

expected.keyTermDefinition: An explanation whose claims are connected to evidence and stated limits.

fields.content:
Colonization involves establishing and maintaining outside authority over a place and its people, beyond a visit or exchange. Economic, political and religious aims were motives; they do not prove results or justify domination. Methods are actions used to pursue aims: force, agreements, offices and religious institutions. Their operation varied. Effects concern consequences for particular people. Intended benefits do not establish everyone’s actual experience. An institution’s creation does not establish universal enforcement, consent or happiness. Separate the source’s claim from what it proves.

Try this fictional report frame: The aim was [aim]. At [place and time], people used [action]. Evidence shows [result], while [claim] still needs evidence.
